claims.claim: The micro:bit 'First lessons' Introduction unit structures every project around a THINK – CREATE – EVALUATE – EXTEND – SHARE framework, used to run each lesson with learners.

The unit explicitly lists 'Evaluate', 'evaluation', 'modifying' and 'prototyping' as additional skills and asks learners to 'Evaluate what you have made', so the young-kids track must keep an explicit Evaluate and Share stage rather than drop it.

Youngest-pitched micro:bit units (Nature art 7-8 yrs, Barefoot wildlife 7-9, Volcano 8-9) use 2-5 short lessons each producing one concrete physical artefact (art, LED animation), so L1-s1..s6 should pace by one tangible make per lesson.

Instructional best practice for young kids favours unplugged, hands-on kinesthetic activities that prime abstract concepts before coding on a screen; L1-s1 should open with a screen-free physical intro.
Young children learn best with one idea per slide and minimal on-screen clutter; lesson slides for L1-s1..s6 should present a single concept (e.g. one block, one input) at a time.
Concrete physical examples beat abstract explanation for ages 6-8; tie each coding idea to a real object/action (button press, heartbeat, step count) the child can see and touch.
Frame debugging as a 'detective game' and celebrate finding/fixing bugs as victories; this maps onto the Evaluate/Extend stage and suits young kids' resilience building.
